name: Mushunguli / Somali Chizigula, with Tanzanian Chizigula
confidence_why: Hout 2020's first-hand dissertation on Mushunguli, Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990 on Tanzanian Chizigula (as quoted in Hyman 2009) and Downing 2004's survey citing Philippson 1998 all describe penultimate prominence that belongs to the phrase, with lengthening only at the end of an utterance in a tonal language, and the only contrary note is Meinhof 1906's impressionistic remark that the accent falls on the antepenult 'at least in many cases'.

catalog_quote: There is a general restriction against the final syllable of an utterance being long, and so compensatory lengthening will fail to apply if word-internal hiatus occurs at the juncture of the penultimate and final syllables of an utterance. ... The lengthening of the penultimate syllable here is due to the fact that this phrase was elicited in isolation: the penultimate syllable of any utterance is also lengthened, as illustrated by the examples in (6). This is usually, but not always, associated with a high pitch target; while penultimate lengthening is quite consistent, tone and intonation are not. (6) Penultimate lengthening a. sidumuːla ‘I chopped’ b. sikemoː m̩ piːra ‘I threw the ball’ c. sikemeː mipira kʷaːmajoːɳ ɖa ‘I threw the balls to the baboons’ Note that nouns elicited in isolation only variably exhibited this lengthening (a possible effect of list intonation), but as the above examples illustrate, nouns can be lengthened in this context. I do not have any examples of multi-clausal sentences in the data I collected; there may be more contexts in which this type of lengthening can occur.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: zigu1244 Zigula-Mushungulu is not in the catalog. All four stress/accent title hits are closed: Kisseberth 1992 (Via Afrika Festschrift, print-only; Google Books snippet only) and Kenstowicz 1989 (Certamen phonologicum, print-only; not on Kenstowicz's MIT page) are the two high-priority acquisitions — both are the primary Tanzanian Chizigula accent/tone analyses; Philippson 1991/92 thesis (theses.fr: accessible = non; abstract read: ~30 East African Bantu languages, penult demarcative accent as evolutionary driver) is medium priority, and its derivative Philippson 1998 (Persée, altcha-gated) is Downing 2004's source for 'Chizigula: penult stress, tonal'; Bamba 1992 (UQAM, 672 pp, not in Archipel) is per a 1992 'Linguistique africaine' snippet a Mande-domain tone-accent thesis with Kizigua and Guéré as extra cases — low priority. Readable first-hand evidence (all already held by the project from the earlier reading, re-read and page-pinned here): Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990:166/171 via Hyman 2009:195 — penult is an abstract accent that attracts H from the left, no stress cues except phrase-final length; Hout 2012:6/49 — penultimate lengthening 'caused by stress assignment' to the utterance penult; Hout 2020:39 — consistent utterance-penult lengthening usually with a high pitch target, tone marginal in Somali Mushunguli; Meinhof 1906:289 (page scan verified) — 'mechanical' stress on the antepenult 'at least in many cases', tone present. Downing 2004:120 codes Chizigula as penult stress-accent + tone. StressTyp2 has no Zigula entry. Recommended coding if added: tonal, penultimate (phrase-final) prominence via tone attraction and lengthening, no lexical word stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence is penultimate: the penult of a word said in isolation / of an utterance is lengthened (extra mora) and usually carries a high pitch target; the utterance-final syllable cannot be long. Hout's earlier thesis (2012: 6, 48) words the same fact as 'Penultimate Lengthening occurs when stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable of an utterance'. For Tanzanian Zigula, Kenstowicz & Kisseberth (1990: 166, quoted verbatim in Hyman 2009: 195) treat the penult as the accented syllable in an abstract sense: it attracts H tone from its left but 'does not have increased duration (except in phrase-final position), nor is it necessarily raised in pitch'. Downing (2004, table 15) codes Chizigula as penult stress-accent, tonal, citing Philippson 1998. Discordant older note: Meinhof (1906: 289) heard the 'mechanische Ton' on the antepenult 'wenigstens in vielen Faellen' (probably the antepenultimate H of some verb tenses, cf. Pillion 2013: a word's H falls on the penult or antepenult).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described in any source examined. (Downing 2004: 129 and K&K 1990 note some H tones shift to the stem-initial syllable in Chizigula, a tonal, not stress, effect.)
new_statements.exceptions: Hout 2020: nouns elicited in isolation only variably show penult lengthening (list intonation); utterance-final syllables are never long (compensatory lengthening blocked there); words inside a phrase lose the lengthening (Hout 2012: 7, mwaana vs mwana ywaangu, with free variation). Meinhof 1906 reports antepenult stress 'in many cases' for Tanzanian Zigula.
new_statements.domain_note: The durational cue is utterance/phrase-level: penult of the utterance (= the word in citation form). Word-internally in Tanzanian Zigula the penult's prominence is tonal (target of H shift) per Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990; Mushunguli (Somali dialect) has largely lost tone (Hout 2020: 50). Citation forms therefore show penult length (+ high pitch); phrase-medial words need not.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 zigu1244 'Zigula-Mushungulu' (ISO ziw) has two dialects: zigu1242 Zigula (Tanzania) and mush1238 Mushungulu = Mushunguli / Somali Chizigula (ISO xma, lower Jubba, Somalia; diaspora in US). The quoted statement (Hout 2020) and Hout 2012 / Pillion 2013 describe the Somali dialect Mushunguli (mush1238), from one primary consultant born in Mogambo; Hout reports tone there is 'at best moribund'. Meinhof 1906 and the tonological literature (Kenstowicz 1989; Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990; Kisseberth 1992) describe Tanzanian Zigula (zigu1242), which is fully tonal with H attracted to the penult. Glottolog lists Hout 2012 and Pillion 2013 as University of Kansas theses; both are Ohio State University B.A. theses (OSU Knowledge Bank).

new_statements.reading: Zigula/Chizigula has penultimate prominence, but of an abstract kind: the penult attracts H tone (long-distance shift, K&K 1990:171) and is lengthened only at utterance/phrase end (Hout 2020:39; Hout 2012:6 calls this 'stress assigned to the penultimate syllable of an utterance'); there is no word-level durational or pitch stress cue. For catalog purposes: tonal language with penultimate (phrase-final) prominence / penult-accent tone attraction, not lexical stress. Meinhof 1906:289 (antepenult 'in many cases') is an early impressionistic outlier. None of the four title-hit items (Kisseberth 1992, Kenstowicz 1989, Philippson 1991, Bamba 1992) is open; Kisseberth 1992 and Kenstowicz 1989 remain the highest-priority acquisitions.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (Hout 2020: penultimate lengthening, tone/intonation variable) and with the on-file synthesis (penult prominence in a tonal language, K&K 1990 via Hyman 2009; Downing 2004 table 'Chizigula: penult, tonal yes (Philippson 1998)'). Adds, from the ultimate source behind Downing's row: (i) the penult culmination in Zigula is one of length and explicitly NOT of pitch (type c, unlike Swahili-type a with both); (ii) Zigula is classed 'sans équivoque' as an accentual(-tonal) language whose H tones are organised in feet that must begin before the penultimate mora (p. 484), i.e. the penult bounds tone displacement; (iii) the system is 'très semblable au giryama' and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Zigula (Tanzanian, G31) is a tone ('accentual') language: lexical H tones survive as at most one H per metrical foot and surface displaced rightward, the foot being bounded by the word's penultimate mora; the penultimate syllable carries the word's prominence as a culmination of LENGTH (penultimate lengthening; the language has no vowel-length contrast), not of pitch. No lexical/contrastive stress placement other than this predictable penult prominence is described.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Zigula. Hedges: Ngulu's membership in the same system is queried ('et le ngulu ?', p. 422); the Zigula material is second-hand in part (Kisseberth & Mochiwa 1986) plus the author's own notes; the general remark (3.5.1, p. 482-484) that penult length culmination is clearest before pause is made for the type, not specifically for Zigula.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Zigula is Tanzanian Zigula (Guthrie G31, groupe XVII 'shambaa, bondei, zigula, ngulu..', own field notes from the 1970s Tanzania survey plus Kisseberth & Mochiwa 1986 on Kizigua of Handeni); the catalog record (Hout 2020) describes Somali Chizigula / Mushunguli, the descendant variety spoken by the Somali Bantu (Gosha) community; Kisbey 1906 describes the Tanzanian (UMCA, Msalabani/Magila area) variety.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The work states no general word-stress rule: its language introduction is historical/classificatory and its phonology page is a letter-to-IPA table with no mention of stress, tone or an accent mark. In the dictionary body the compilers treat Chizigula words as carrying a word stress with an implicit default position and flag about fifteen items (almost all loanwords: Kánada, tétano, táitoli, Ráshiya, Chiráshiya, malériya, Malésiya, shíngiya, jénisi, áshito; plus the adjective stem -hya 'new' whose stress sits on the prefix vowel, and uhya/ihya) whose stress is initial, antepenultimate or on the prefix, writing it with an acute accent in headword variants and example sentences. Every flagged exception is pre-penultimate; none flags penultimate stress as special, which is consistent with (but does not state) a penultimate default. Two particles (tú, twé) get tone notes (high vs mid tone).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing beyond the phrase 'primary stress' in the notes on hya/mphya/uhya (implying other syllables are less prominent); no secondary-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions marked with acute and a Phon note: initial/first-syllable stress in kanada, tetano, taitoli (< Eng), Rashiya, shingiya, jenisi (pl. majénisi), ashito (< It), uhya, ihya ('The first vowel is always stressed: [íhya]'), mphya ('primary stress is on the initial m-'); antepenultimate in Chirashiya, Warashiya; 'second syllable é' in maleriya (< It), Malesiya; stress on the preceding prefix vowel for -hya 'new' (wáhya, chíhya, kwíhya). Tone: tú 'always has a high tone', onomatopoeic twe with mid vs high tone.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary describes Chizigula of Somalia (ISO xma, 'Mushungulu'), as spoken by Somali Bantu refugees resettled in Boise, Idaho; its introduction states that Somali Chizigula is 'substantially different' from Tanzanian Kizigula (G31, ziw), with 40-50% of Kisbey 1907's Tanzanian headwords absent from their corpus. Glottolog zigu1244 covers both varieties; the stress notes apply to the Somali variety only.

tone_statements.citation: MacSaveny, Erin (2009). Verbal tone in Chizigula. Occasional Papers in Applied Linguistics (OPAL) 5. pp. 1-7.
tone_statements.quote: The tonal system of Chizigula (Bantu) includes both lexical and grammatical tone, which interact in complex ways when they co-occur on verbs. When a verb has two H tones, the final H surfaces on the penultimate syllable, while the initial H associates to the first stem syllable and spreads rightward. A L tone is inserted between two H’s as a result of the OCP, and this L tone surfaces on the antepenult and blocks the spread of the first H; on trisyllabic stems, it cannot associate and instead causes downstep. ... Verb roots in Chizigula may belong to one of two tone classes. They are either underlyingly toneless, or they carry a lexical H tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 1: Abstract, and sec. 2 'Verb roots with H tone' (examples (1)-(2) ku-damanya 'to do' vs ku-lombéza 'to ask'); stress assumption p. 1 sec. 2; downstep p. 5-6; conclusion sec. 4 p. 6-7

readall_conflicts: The only conflict on record is the one already noted in the on-disk check: Meinhof 1906 (MSOS 9, sec. 8 Betonung, p. 289) gives antepenultimate stress 'in many cases' for Tanzanian Zigula, against the penultimate prominence reported by Kenstowicz & Kisseberth 1990 (via Hyman 2009:195), Downing 2004 table (15) citing Philippson 1998, and Hout 2020:39 for Mushunguli; our earlier reading treats Meinhof as an early impressionistic outlier. The Philippson 1992 abstract is compatible with the penultimate reading but says nothing about Zigula itself.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. sources.note: Second-hand but verbatim from the primary Tanzanian Chizigula source: the penultimate syllable is the prominent ('accented') position — H tone shifts long-distance to the penult — but this accent is abstract: no durational cue except phrase-finally and no obligatory pitch raising. Auch scheint es mir, daß die Vokale viel kürzer abgerissen werden als im Suaheli. Der musikalische Ton ist, so viel ich sehe, nachzuweisen. [EN: As regards stress, note that the dynamic accent here lies not, as in Swahili, on the penultimate but on the antepenultimate, at least in many cases. sources.note: Earliest first-hand statement (Tanzanian Zigula, 1906): dynamic stress on the antepenult 'in many cases', contrasting with Swahili penult; tone present. Conflicts with the modern penult-prominence analyses (K&K 1990; Hout 2012/2020) — likely reflects H-tone attraction to the penult being heard as antepenult prominence, or phrase-medial vs isolation forms; treat as historical, superseded.

tone.quote: The tonal system of Chizigula (Bantu) includes both lexical and grammatical tone, which interact in complex ways when they co-occur on verbs. When a verb has two H tones, the final H surfaces on the penultimate syllable, while the initial H associates to the first stem syllable and spreads rightward. A L tone is inserted between two H’s as a result of the OCP, and this L tone surfaces on the antepenult and blocks the spread of the first H; on trisyllabic stems, it cannot associate and instead causes downstep. ... Verb roots in Chizigula may belong to one of two tone classes. They are either underlyingly toneless, or they carry a lexical H tone.
